Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors

Robin Shing Moon Chan Affiliation: ETH Zürich Email: robin.chan@inf.ethz.ch    Ryan Cotterell Affiliation: ETH Zürich Email: ryan.cotterell@inf.ethz.ch
Abstract

Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input–output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input–output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input–output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior p0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}} over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input–output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after 𝒪⁡(1γ​log⁡1/p0​(f⋆)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}}(\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log 1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})) informative oracle queries, and returns the target program f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 2222 percentage points while observing up to 10.510.5 fewer input–output examples.

https://github.com/chanr0/interactive-program-induction

1 Introduction

Many domain experts have a computer program clearly in mind that encodes certain rule-based behavior, but they cannot easily write it down themselves. For instance, a spreadsheet user often knows how they would like the column of names to be reformatted, but cannot write the regex. Similarly, a linguist knows how a sentence in their native language should be segmented, but cannot program the tokenizer. Inductive programming, also known as programming by example (Summers, 1977; Lieberman, 2001; Gulwani et al., 2012; Gulwani et al., 2017), aims to bridge this gap by recovering the program from input–output examples. The paradigm has been deployed at scale for specific applications, most prominently in Microsoft Excel’s FlashFill (Gulwani, 2011).

However, recovering a target program from finite input–output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, since any finite set of examples is consistent with infinitely many programs that diverge on unseen data. Without an inductive bias, it is unclear which to choose (Solomonoff, 1964). Prior work restricts the program space to a hand-designed domain-specific language (DSL) (Shapiro, 1983; Gulwani et al., 2017), at the cost of expressivity (cf. App. A). Within a DSL, the consistent programs can be enumerated, and the target one selected through human feedback, for instance by asking for further examples (Mayer et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2020), or through an oracle in place of a human (Solar-Lezama, 2008; Jha et al., 2010). Large language models trained on code (Chen et al., 2021; Austin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022) may help to go beyond DSLs by providing distributions over programs in a general-purpose language (e.g., Python). Still, when used as one-shot program inductors, they offer few mechanisms or guarantees for selecting the target among the many consistent programs. Li & Ellis (2024) report a substantial gap to hand-engineered systems on programming-by-example, and Wei et al. (2025) report limited success of LLM agents doing autonomous program induction in Python with oracle feedback.

In this work, we propose an algorithm for interactive program induction over a general-purpose programming language, and derive theoretical guarantees on the number of oracle queries it requires and on the accuracy of the recovered program. To this end, we treat the target program as the unknown of a Bayesian inference problem, with a language model prior p0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}} over programs as inductive bias and a posterior that concentrates on f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} as input–output examples are observed, and we choose which inputs to query by sequential Bayesian experimental design (Lindley, 1956; MacKay, 1992; Grand et al., 2026; Kobalczyk et al., 2025). Using a notion of approximate equivalence between programs (Rice, 1953, exact equivalence being undecidable,) and an expected information gain criterion for query selection, we show that the algorithm terminates after 𝒪⁡(1γ​log⁡1/p0​(f⋆)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}}(\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log 1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})) queries when every answer carries at least γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} bits. Dasgupta (2004) analyzed this greedy rule over finite hypothesis classes, and our analysis carries over to programs because we measure agreement on a finite sample of inputs. Conditional on returning the target’s equivalence class, the returned program is approximately correct with high probability. Finally, we evaluate the practical implications on the CodeARC program induction dataset (Wei et al., 2025) and show that the algorithm improves accuracy over the CodeARC LM agent while reducing the number of required oracle calls in most evaluated settings.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate interactive program induction in a general-purpose language as Bayesian active learning. Since the posterior over programs is intractable and program equivalence is undecidable, we approximate the posterior, and with it the expected information gain, by importance sampling with a language model as prior and proposal (§ 4), and replace exact equivalence by agreement on a finite sample of inputs (§ 2.2).

  • •

    When every answer carries at least γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} bits, we bound the number of queries by 𝒪⁡(1γ​log⁡1/p0​(f⋆)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}}(\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log 1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})) per instance for any selection rule, and by the prior entropy over γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} in expectation for the greedy rule. We characterize when a wrong class is returned and give a PAC bound on the error (§ 3).

  • •

    On CodeARC, our method improves accuracy over the LM-only agent on most evaluated language models, by up to 2222 percentage points with up to 10.510.5 fewer input–output examples. Controls attribute the gains to the selection criterion and the importance weights (§ 5, § E.4). We find that the miscalibration of the language model prior limits the accuracy of the method (Fig. 3).

2 Information-Theoretic Program Induction

We formalize interactive program induction as the problem of recovering a target function f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} from input–output observations that are revealed incrementally. Let X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X} be a countable set of inputs and Y{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y} a countable set of outputs, and let the target f⋆:X→Y{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}\colon{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y} be an unknown but fixed element of the candidate space YX{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}}}. We observe f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} only through its behavior on selected inputs. At each round t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} we choose an input x(t)∈X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}, the query, and obtain its output y(t)=f⋆​(x(t)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}) from the oracle. Our goal is to return a function f^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}} that closely approximates f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} after as few queries as possible.

2.1 Setup

A finite sample of input–output pairs does not pin down a target in YX{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}}}, since infinitely many functions agree on any finite subset of X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X} and disagree elsewhere (Solomonoff, 1964). Recovering f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} therefore requires two pieces of additional structure, which together turn this ill-posed recovery problem into a well-posed Bayesian inference problem. The first is a program prior p0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}} over YX{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}}}, which encodes the inductive bias. Many functions are consistent with a finite observation set, and the prior determines which of them are a priori plausible. The second is an input distribution μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} over X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}, specifying the population of inputs on which the recovered function should agree with f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}. The program prior decides which functions we prefer, and the input distribution decides where agreement is measured. We assume that programs are deterministic and that p0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}} has countable support with p0​(f⋆)>0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})>0. Whether a program halts on an input is undecidable, so evaluating whether it reproduces an observed output may not terminate. We therefore run every program with a time limit, and a program that raises or exceeds this limit on an input returns a distinguished error output, so every program defines a function on all of X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}. In the setting most relevant to this work (program synthesis over strings, where X=Y=Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}}) the input distribution μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} has countably infinite support. Comparing a candidate against f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} on every input in this support is infeasible, and even integrating against μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} to estimate disagreement requires structure we do not assume. In the following, we derive the approximate notions of equivalence we use throughout.

2.2 Approximate Equivalence

Two facts about the interactive setting force us to relax exact program equivalence. First, exact equivalence of two computable functions is undecidable (Rice, 1953), so no algorithm can take two such functions and decide whether they agree on every input. Second, two functions can be compared on any single input by running them, but the query budget is finite while X{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X} is typically infinite, so agreement on every input cannot be certified by exhaustive testing. We therefore want an equivalence relation that (i) measures disagreement under the population μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} and (ii) can be certified by inspecting only finitely many inputs. The first relaxation accomplishes (i) by declaring f{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f} equivalent to f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} when their disagreement under μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} is small. For ϵ∈(0,1){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}\in(0,1),

f∼ϵf⋆⇔errμ(f)≤ϵ,errμ(f)=defPrx∼μ[f(x)≠f⋆(x)].\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}\sim_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}\iff{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{err}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f})\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon},\qquad{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{err}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}\Pr_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})\neq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})]. f∼Sf⋆⇔f(x)=f⋆(x) for all x∈S.\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}\sim_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}\iff{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})\text{ for all }{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}. (2)

2.3 Bayesian Updating

With the equivalence relation in place, we set up the Bayesian inference machinery on which our query selection rule will operate.

2.4 Greedy Information Gain Algorithm

We now describe an algorithm that constructs 𝒟1,𝒟2,…{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{1},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{2},\ldots by selecting a maximally informative query x(t)∈S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} at a time. Queries are selected from S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} because that is where the classes are defined. All programs in a class return the same output on every x∈S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, so the answer to such a query eliminates whole classes and never splits one, and the posterior stays a distribution over the same classes. Any two distinct classes disagree on some x∈S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, so queries in S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} suffice to identify [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}}. Each query is chosen by the expected information gain criterion of Bayesian experimental design (Lindley, 1956; MacKay, 1992), with the equivalence class of the target as the quantity of interest. More precisely, at each round t=1,2,…{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}=1,2,\ldots:

  1. 1.

    Select. Choose the input x(t)∈S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} that maximizes the expected information gain (Shannon, 1948; MacKay, 1992) with respect to p∼(⋅∣𝒟t−1){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1}),

    x(t)=argmaxx∈SH[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t−1)]−∑y∈Yp(y∣x,𝒟t−1)H[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t−1∪{(x,y)})],\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}=\argmax_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}\!\bigl[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1})\bigr]-\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}Y}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1})\,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}\!\bigl[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1}\cup\{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y})\})\bigr], (7)

    where H⁡[⋅]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}[\cdot] denotes the Shannon entropy and p(⋅∣x,𝒟t−1){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1}) is the posterior predictive of Eq. 5b.

  2. 2.

    Query. Observe y(t)=f⋆​(x(t)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}) and set 𝒟t=𝒟t−1∪{(x(t),y(t))}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}-1}\cup\{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})})\}.

  3. 3.

    Update. Compute p(⋅∣𝒟t){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}) via Eq. 5a and the pushforward p∼(⋅∣𝒟t){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}) via Eq. 6.

Terminate at the first round t≥0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}\geq 0 such that some class c^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}} reaches majority pushforward mass, i.e., when p∼​(c^∣𝒟t)>12{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})>\tfrac{1}{2}, and return any f^∈c^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}}\in\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}}. Both are stated in terms of the entropy of the prior over classes and of the information a round is guaranteed to yield, which depends on the queries available in the evaluation set and on which of them the selection strategy picks.

Theorem 3.1 bounds the number of queries in expectation over targets drawn from the prior. It is specific to the greedy rule, whose query has the largest expected information in S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} and therefore at least γ¯t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bar{\gamma}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}, the largest guaranteed information any query in S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} offers. Theorem 3.2 bounds the number of queries for a fixed target program. Its proof does not use the greedy rule, so the bound applies to every selection rule over S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} with the guaranteed information of that rule’s own queries, and § 5 empirically evaluates several such rules. In both, the rate of convergence is set by γ¯t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bar{\gamma}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} over S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} and γt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} at the selected query, which are determined by how the program prior spreads mass across classes and how finely S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, drawn from the input distribution, separates them.

Improvement over non-adaptive querying.

Fix a target error ϵ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon} and confidence δ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\delta}. A non-adaptive strategy draws inputs at random from μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}, has the oracle label all of them, and accepts a program that agrees with the target on every one. It needs Ω⁡(log⁡(1/δ)/ϵ)\Omega(\log(1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\delta})/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}) labeled inputs, since a program that disagrees with f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} on a set of μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}-mass ϵ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon} passes mm random inputs with probability (1−ϵ)m≥e−2​m​ϵ(1-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon})^{m}\geq e^{-2m{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}} for ϵ≤12{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}\leq\tfrac{1}{2} (Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David, 2014, see, e.g.,), and by Prop. 2.1 inputs of that order also suffice, up to the ln⁡(1/p0​(f))\ln(1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f})) term. The greedy algorithm needs an evaluation set of the same size, but the oracle labels only the T≤N{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}T}\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N} inputs it queries. Since f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} lies in its own class, that class has prior mass at least p0​(f⋆){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}) whatever S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} is, so under the hypotheses of Thm. 3.2 the algorithm asks at most ⌊1γ​log2​12​p0​(f⋆)⌋+1\lfloor\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log_{2}\tfrac{1}{2{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})}\rfloor+1 queries, a number that does not depend on ϵ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}. The non-adaptive cost grows with 1/ϵ1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\epsilon}, while the adaptive cost is set by how plausible the target is under the prior. The PAC certificate of Prop. 2.1 then holds for the returned program, conditional on the algorithm returning the target’s class.

The role of |S||{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}|.

Combining Prop. 2.1 with Thms. 3.1 and 3.2 gives a complete guarantee. The greedy algorithm terminates after at most ⌊1γ​log2​12​p∼​([f⋆]∼∣𝒟0)⌋+1\lfloor\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log_{2}\tfrac{1}{2{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{0})}\rfloor+1 queries when every answer carries at least γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} bits, for a target drawn from the prior it returns the target’s class with probability p∼​(c^∣𝒟T)>12{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}T})>\tfrac{1}{2}, and since Prop. 2.1 holds for every program in [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}} simultaneously, the returned program satisfies Pr[errμ(f^)>(ln(1/p0(f^))+ln(1/δ))/N]≤Pr[c^≠[f⋆]∼]+δ\Pr[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{err}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}}}(\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}})>(\ln(1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}(\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}}))+\ln(1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\delta}))/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N}]\leq\Pr[\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}}\neq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}}]+{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\delta}. The size of the evaluation set enters the two bounds in opposite directions. A larger S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} makes the error bound tighter, but it also refines ∼\sim, so the target’s class shrinks, its prior mass decreases, and the query bound grows. We evaluate the effect of |S||{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}| empirically in Section 5.

4 Approximate Inference with a Language Model

The greedy algorithm of § 2.4 requires the pushforward entropy H[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t)]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})], a sum over equivalence classes weighted by posterior mass. The posterior is a distribution over the countably infinite support of the prior, so neither it nor this sum can be computed exactly. We approximate the posterior by a weighted set of programs sampled from a language model, and compute the pushforward from the weights.

4.1 Language Model Proposal

Language model preliminaries.

An alphabet Σ{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}} is a finite, non-empty set of symbols, Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}} the set of all strings 𝒙{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}} formed from Σ{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}} (including the empty string), and |𝒙||{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}| the length of 𝒙{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}. A language model pLM{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}} is a probability distribution over Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}}. The prefix probability p→LM​(𝒙)=def∑𝒙′∈Σ∗pLM​(𝒙​𝒙′){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}\sum_{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}^{\prime}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}\,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}^{\prime}) is the probability that a string drawn from pLM{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}} begins with 𝒙{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}. Whenever p→LM​(𝒙)>0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})>0, the conditional prefix probability is

p→LM​(𝒙′∣𝒙)=def{pLM​(𝒙)/p→LM​(𝒙)if ​𝒙′=□,p→LM​(𝒙​𝒙′)/p→LM​(𝒙)otherwise,\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}^{\prime}\mid{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}\begin{cases}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})&\text{if }{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}^{\prime}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\raisebox{-0.2pt}{${\square}$}},\\ {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}\,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}^{\prime})/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (9)

where □∉Σ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\raisebox{-0.2pt}{${\square}$}}\notin{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}} is a distinguished end-of-string delimiter. Iterating Eq. 9 yields the autoregressive factorization

pLM​(𝒙)=p→LM​(□∣𝒙)​∏t=1|𝒙|p→LM​(xt∣𝒙<t),\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\raisebox{-0.2pt}{${\square}$}}\mid{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})\prod_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}=1}^{|{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}|}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\vec{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}\mid{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}_{<{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}}), (10)

which computes pLM​(𝒙){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}) from |𝒙|+1|{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}|+1 next-token queries without enumerating Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}}. The same definitions apply to a language model conditioned on a context string.

Proposal over programs.

An LM is a distribution over strings, but our algorithm needs distributions over programs. We obtain them by prompting the LM with input–output examples and asking for a program consistent with them (App. F gives the prompts), so that its distribution over completions is a distribution over source code. Strictly, this makes pLM{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}} a distribution over implementations, whereas a program is an input–output behavior, and two distinct strings 𝒙1≠𝒙2{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}_{1}\neq{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}_{2} may decode to the same function while pLM​(𝒙1)≠pLM​(𝒙2){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}_{1})\neq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}_{2}). The equivalence relation ∼\sim from § 2.2 and the pushforward p∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}} from § 2.3 collapse implementations that agree on S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} into a single class, so the algorithm operates at the level of programs, indifferent to syntactic differences between implementations, while sampling and density evaluation happen at the level of implementations, where Eq. 10 makes them tractable.

At each round t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} we encode the observed examples into a prompt (Chan et al., 2024), a context string prompt⁡(𝒟t)∈Σ∗{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{prompt}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}} (App. F), and condition the LM on it. Its completions are implementations 𝒙∈Σ∗{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Sigma}}^{*}}, each of which decodes to a function by execution. The proposal over implementations is

qt​(𝒙)=defpLM​(𝒙∣prompt⁡(𝒟t)),\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}})\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}_{\mathrm{LM}}}({{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\bm{x}}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{prompt}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})), (11)

and we take the program prior to be the proposal before any query, p0=defq0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{def}}}{{=}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{0}. The fixed objects p0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}} and μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} define the guarantees of § 3, while the proposal qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} is an approximation mechanism whose quality affects practical efficiency but not the guarantees for the exact posterior.

4.2 Importance Sampling Estimates

Importance weights.

We draw M{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M} implementations from qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}, write f1,…,fM{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{1},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M} for their decoded functions and p0​(fm){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}), qt​(fm){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}) for the densities of the sampled implementations, and assign self-normalizing importance weights

wm=p0(fm)⋅∏(x,y)∈𝒟t𝟙{fm(x)=y}qt​(fm).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}w}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}=\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m})\cdot\prod_{({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y})\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}}\mathbbm{1}\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}\}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m})}. (12)

Programs inconsistent with the observed data 𝒟t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} receive zero weight. For consistent programs, p0​(fm)/qt​(fm){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m})/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}) corrects for the mismatch between prior and proposal. Because qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} is already conditioned on 𝒟t{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}, it concentrates on consistent programs. At round 00 the weights reduce to the consistency indicator, since p0=q0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{0}. Density ratios enter only when particles are resampled from a later qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}. Both densities are then the probability the LM assigns to the extracted code block under the respective prompt, without the reasoning that precedes it and without the sampling temperature. The weights are therefore an approximation to Eq. 12, which we do because intermediate reasoning and a tuned sampling temperature improve the sampled programs (§ E.6). Section E.4 compares them to the exact weights of the sampled completions and to uniform weights. The approximate and exact weights perform on par, and both require significantly fewer input–output examples than uniform weights.

Pushforward mass.

The pushforward mass on a class c{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c} is a posterior expectation, p∼(c∣𝒟t)=𝔼f∼p(⋅∣𝒟t)[𝟙{f∈c}]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})}[\mathbbm{1}\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\}], which the self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) estimator (Owen, 2013) replaces by the weighted share of the particles in the class,

p^∼(c∣𝒟t)=∑m:fm∈cwm∑m=1Mwm,\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}}_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})=\frac{\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}:\,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}w}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}}{\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}=1}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}w}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}}, (13)

where class membership is checked by comparing outputs on S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, as two programs share a ∼\sim-class if and only if they agree on every x∈S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}.

Entropy and information gain.

Plugging Eq. 13 into the definition of entropy gives the plug-in estimator

H^[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t)]=−∑cp^∼(c∣𝒟t)log2p^∼(c∣𝒟t).\displaystyle\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})]=-\sum_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}}_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})\log_{2}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}}_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}). (14)

The information gain for a candidate query x{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x} is estimated by partitioning the particles by predicted output fm​(x){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}), computing H^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}} on each partition with renormalized weights, and weighting by the estimated posterior predictive

p^(y∣x,𝒟t)=∑m:fm​(x)=ywm∑m=1Mwm.\displaystyle\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})=\frac{\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}:\,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x})={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}y}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}w}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}}{\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}=1}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}w}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}}. (15)

The greedy step of § 2.4 is a finite maximization over S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, with H^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}} in place of H{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}} and p^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}} in place of p{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}. Algorithm 1 summarizes the resulting procedure, with an effective-sample-size test that redraws the particles from the current proposal when the weights degenerate.

Approximation gaps.

Under absolute continuity of the posterior with respect to qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} (i.e., p⁡(f∣𝒟t)>0⟹qt​(f)>0{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})>0\implies{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f})>0), exact weights, and finitely many classes, the SNIS estimates p^∼​(c∣𝒟t){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}}}_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}) converge to p∼​(c∣𝒟t){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}) as M→∞{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M}\to\infty (Owen, 2013, e.g.,), and since H^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}} is continuous in these estimates, H^[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t)]→H[p∼(⋅∣𝒟t)]\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})]\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{H}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{\sim}}(\cdot\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t})] by the continuous mapping theorem. The guarantees of § 3 are stated for the exact posterior, and for finite M{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M} two things can go wrong. The particles may miss [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}} entirely, or a wrong class may exceed the threshold before enough of them land in [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}}, which the miscalibration of the prior makes common (Fig. 3). Section E.5 varies the particle budget, and Tab. 4 and App. B quantify how many runs terminate on a wrong class or without a consistent program.

5 Experiments

We now evaluate the practical implications of our work on a programming induction benchmark in Python (Wei et al., 2025, CodeARC;). Its reference method, which we call the CodeARC LM agent, prompts a language model to autonomously choose the inputs to query, propose an implementation, and terminate when it feels confident, with no posterior over programs and no criterion for the choice of inputs. Our experiments aim to address four questions.

  1. RQ1.

    Does Alg. 1 improve accuracy and oracle cost over the CodeARC LM agent?

  2. RQ2.

    Does EIG ask queries with more guaranteed information than other selection criteria, and how much do the queries add over the prior alone?

  3. RQ3.

    How does the choice of evaluation set size N{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N} trade off convergence and correctness, as hypothesized in § 3?

  4. RQ4.

    What are the failure modes of language model priors in program induction?

5.1 Setup

Dataset.

We evaluate the proposed approach on the inductive inference benchmark CodeARC (Wei et al., 2025), whose 11141114 Python functions are drawn from HumanEval+, MBPP+, and APPS and range from 22 to 7474 lines, from entry-level tasks to competition problems. Similarly to our setup, the benchmark simulates an inductive inference scenario where a language modeling agent needs to find diverse Python functions from input–output pairs through membership queries (MQ), which query f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} on a chosen input x{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x} to obtain f⋆​(x){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}x}), and equivalence queries (EQ), which ask the oracle whether a candidate f^\widehat{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f}} equals f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} and return a counterexample if it does not, under a fixed MQ and EQ invocation budget.11 1 We note that our setup is equivalent to the CodeARC setup if the EQ budget is 1. We use the anonymized split, which replaces all function names with a generic identifier and so suppresses any cues for the program prior. Following Wei et al. (2025), we provide a small number of seed invocations (initial input–output examples that we also use to condition μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}), evaluating both 11 and 1010 seed invocations, and set the query budget to 3030 input–output pairs, which includes the seed invocations. For consistency with their results, the CodeARC agent may additionally issue 22 equivalence queries, while our algorithm makes none and submits its returned program once for evaluation. We evaluate on the full split and report means over 55 independent seed runs. The input distribution μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} fixes the inputs on which agreement with f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} is measured, and with it what equivalence means. It is part of the problem and independent of the seed invocations shown, so we condition it on all 1010 seed invocations of the benchmark and keep it fixed across settings (App. D). For the models that overlap with Wei et al. (2025), we reproduce their reported results within seed noise.

Models.

We evaluate our algorithm on six models of various sizes: Llama3.2-3B and Llama3.1-8B (Llama Team, 2024), Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B (Yang et al., 2025), Olmo3-7B (Team Olmo et al., 2025), and Ministral-8B (Mistral AI team, 2024). We use the instruction-tuned variant of every model. We chose these models for their differing performance on the CodeARC benchmark.

Baselines and Evaluation.

To test whether our algorithm converges efficiently on the target program, we compare it to the full CodeARC baselines in terms of average number of input–output examples observed and accuracy upon termination. CodeARC equivalence queries give the baseline strictly more oracle access than our method when the EQ budget exceeds 1, so CodeARC @ 2 EQ is a more powerful oracle setting. Following Wei et al. (2025), we evaluate the correctness of the generated programs extrinsically using the differential testing tool Mokav (Etemadi et al., 2025). We fix Mokav’s test-generating language model to Qwen2.5-32B, the best-performing model, for all evaluated models and both methods, so that accuracies are comparable across models.

5.2 Results

RQ1: Algorithm 1 with EIG improves accuracy and query efficiency over the LM only agent.

Tab. 1 shows that the proposed method improves over the LM only (CodeARC) agent in most of the evaluated settings in terms of the final accuracy (up to +.22+.22) as well as oracle querying efficiency (up to 10.510.5 fewer input–output examples). A gap to perfect accuracy remains, which we attribute to the models’ general performance ceiling in proposing valid code matching the shown input–output pairs (cf. Wei et al. (2025), and our failure mode analysis in Tab. 4). Aside from this, the method commonly struggles with early termination due to early posterior concentration (RQ4), which is the case Thm. 3.2 excludes, a heavier class that stays consistent with every answer. Our ablation in Fig. 5 shows that the choice of proposal prompt and temperature reduces this.

RQ2: EIG asks the most informative queries and terminates in the fewest rounds, at an accuracy within noise of the other criteria.

The termination panels of Fig. 1 condition on runs whose initial particles contain the target’s class, for all strategies alike. Compared to the other selection criteria within the proposed algorithm, EIG selects the most informative queries, .70.70 to .99.99 guaranteed bits per query against .31.31 to .52.52 for diversity and random selection, terminates in the fewest rounds, and reaches an accuracy within the seed intervals of the best criterion for every model (Fig. 1, Tab. 6). The queries yield a significant improvement over two controls, prior majority, which returns a program from the majority class of the initial particles without any query, and the CodeARC agent, which selects its queries heuristically (Tabs. 1 and 6). Table 5 reports the bound of Thm. 3.2 on the EIG runs, which is attained in .37.37 of them. Section E.4 further compares against uniform weights, minimax selection, and a compute-matched propose-and-verify baseline.

RQ3: Larger S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} makes convergence on the target’s class rarer but more reliable.

Figure 3 presents an ablation of the evaluation set size N{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N} from 2 to 256 for three models. As predicted in Section 3, a smaller N{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N} makes [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}} coarse, since equivalence then requires agreement on only a few inputs. The posterior concentrates early on such a coarse class, and the program returned from it is often rejected by the oracle despite agreeing with f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} on S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}. As S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} grows, convergence on [f⋆]∼{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}}]_{\sim}} becomes rarer but a reliable indicator of correctness. The rising conditional accuracy instantiates Prop. 2.1, since agreement with f⋆{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}} on more sampled inputs means fewer disagreements on unseen ones.

RQ4: The language model prior is miscalibrated.

Figure 3 is a calibration plot of the prior majority class against the CodeARC targets.22 2 The CodeARC targets may not coincide with the programs humans would consider plausible, against which the prior may be calibrated differently. For every model, the majority class is the target’s class far less often than its prior mass suggests. The prior is thus confident early, while Bayesian inductive inference relies on the prior to keep alternatives plausible until the data rule them out. By Thm. 3.2, a run converges on a wrong program if the prior strongly favors a wrong class, which this miscalibration makes common (Tab. 4).

6 Conclusion

We presented a Bayesian active-learning approach for efficient program induction with oracle feedback that uses a language model as both the program prior and the importance-sampling proposal. We proved that the greedy information-gain algorithm terminates after 𝒪⁡(1γ​log⁡1/p0​(f⋆)){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}}(\tfrac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma}}\log 1/{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f^{\star}})) oracle invocations when every answer carries at least γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} bits, and introduced an equivalence relation that yields a PAC certificate on population error. Empirically, the algorithm improves accuracy and reduces oracle calls over the CodeARC agent in most evaluated settings, and its queries improve over returning the prior’s majority class. We see this work as a step toward principled human-in-the-loop program induction, where the same framework can accommodate richer oracle models, such as noisy users, and structured priors.

Appendix A Related Work

Interactive and oracle-guided program synthesis.

Early works in oracle-guided program synthesis include CEGIS (Solar-Lezama, 2008), and is formalized in works by Jha et al. (2010) and Jha & Seshia (2017), where an automated verifier supplies counterexamples in place of a human. Interactive disambiguation with human oracles was deployed in FlashFill by Mayer et al. (2015) and studied theoretically by Ji et al. (2020), who select questions by minimax over programs sampled from a PCFG posterior over a version space. Tiwari et al. (2020) select inputs that maximize the entropy of the outputs of sampled programs, weighted by a ranking heuristic. All of these operate over a finite DSL and use heuristic or symbolic distinguishability criteria. We work over a countably infinite program space and derive query-complexity bounds from the program prior.

Active learning for program synthesis.

Barnaby et al. (2025) discuss active learning in the neurosymbolic setting, where neural components can mispredict and cause convergence failures. Their constrained conformal evaluation is complementary to our work, which assumes a symbolic target and bounds query complexity information-theoretically. Our query-selection criterion is an instance of Bayesian experimental design (Lindley, 1956; MacKay, 1992), applied sequentially as in active learning (Settles, 2012). Dasgupta (2004) showed that greedy information-gain maximization over a finite class uses at most 4​ln⁡(1/minh⁡p0​(h))4\ln(1/\min_{h}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p}}^{0}}(h)) times the expected number of queries of the optimal strategy. We bound the number of queries of the greedy rule over a countable program space by measuring agreement on a finite sample of inputs, and replace enumeration with importance sampling under an LM proposal. Our query bounds depend on the size of the evaluation set, because a larger set separates more programs into distinct classes. A finite hypothesis class has no such dependence. Golovin et al. (2010), Golovin & Krause (2011), and Nowak (2011) show that greedy rules over finite classes use nearly as few queries as the best possible adaptive plan of queries, which is intractable to compute. We bound the number of queries directly and make no such theoretical comparison.

Bayesian program induction.

Bayesian priors over programs underlie a long line of work. Lake et al. (2015) used hand-designed generative models over strokes for few-shot concept learning, Ellis et al. (2021) bootstrapped reusable libraries via wake-sleep inference, Ellis et al. (2022) applied the same framework to linguistic theory synthesis, and Saad et al. (2019) sampled probabilistic programs from PCFG posteriors. These systems trade expressivity for tractability through a hand-crafted DSL or generative model. We keep the Bayesian perspective but substitute a language model for the hand-crafted prior, using importance sampling to make inference tractable over an unrestricted program space. Singhal et al. (2026) use a language model to propose programs for empirical risk minimization on a fixed sample and give generalization guarantees. We select the examples interactively.

Information-seeking questions with language models.

Several works select questions by expected information gain over hypotheses sampled from a language model, for natural-language rules on a Zendo-style task (Piriyakulkij et al., 2024), task disambiguation including code generation (Kobalczyk et al., 2025), collaborative search games (Grand et al., 2026), and natural-language database querying (Chan et al., 2026). Lee et al. (2025) select inputs by maximin over the outputs of language-model-sampled programs, with a language model predicting outputs in place of the oracle. Kobalczyk et al. (2025) and Lee et al. (2025) treat sampled hypotheses as equally likely. We weight them by importance sampling under an explicit program prior. We apply this idea to program induction with an input–output oracle and derive query-complexity and correctness guarantees under an explicit program prior.

LLMs for program synthesis.

LLMs achieve strong results on natural-language-specified code generation (Chen et al., 2021; Austin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022) but struggle with programming by example without domain-specific fine-tuning (Li & Ellis, 2024). HySynth (Barke et al., 2024) extracts a task-specific PCFG from LLM samples to guide bottom-up enumerative search, and Li et al. (2024) pursue a similar direction using syntactic guidance. Both treat the LM as a one-shot prior over a fixed DSL, without user interaction or posterior updating. Grouping sampled programs by their outputs on a set of inputs is used to select a submission in AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022), CodeT (Chen et al., 2023), and MBR-exec (Shi et al., 2022), and our equivalence relation ∼S\sim_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} is the same construction. Wei et al. (2025) introduced CodeARC, an interactive benchmark where agents iteratively query a hidden oracle and input selection is left to the agent’s heuristics. We use the LM as a prior and importance sampling proposal within a Bayesian framework and choose oracle membership queries to maximize expected information gain.

Appendix B Limitations

Computational cost.

Each round of the algorithm requires potentially drawing M{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M} program samples from the LM proposal qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t}, evaluating each on the inputs in S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S}, and recomputing importance weights and entropy estimates over the candidate pool. Larger evaluation sets, larger particle budgets, and longer programs all compound this cost, and the per-round latency is dominated by LM inference. Tab. 2 reports the cost per problem. Alg. 1 makes 3232 to 7878 LM calls and samples about 110110 candidate programs, each of which it executes on S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} and on every query, against 55 to 1010 calls for the agent. Its wall-clock time per problem is nevertheless below the agent’s in our setup, since the agent’s calls are long generations and it keeps querying for most of its budget. The query-efficiency gains we report are savings in oracle effort, and the compute cost is in LM calls and program executions. Finally, the importance weights at resampling require the LM’s token log-probabilities of a program under two prompts, which closed APIs may not expose.

Dependence on the input distribution.

Proposition 2.1 bounds the error under the input distribution μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}, which we instantiate by prompting an LM with the seed examples. A single seed invocation suffices for the gains of Tab. 1, and rebuilding the evaluation set from the single visible seed example changes accuracy by at most .02.02 on five of six models (App. D). The bound does not guarantee generalization beyond μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}. A differential tester searches for a counterexample and may find one on an input that μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} rarely produces, so the accuracies we report also measure how well agreement under μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu} generalizes. A prompt that describes the intended inputs more closely improves this generalization.

Gap between theoretical and empirical correctness.

Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 hold for the exact posterior. The algorithm works with a finite particle approximation of it, and with priors that are sometimes concentrated on a wrong class. Both account for the .34.34 to .63.63 of runs in Tab. 4 that converge on a wrong program, since a wrong class can exceed the threshold before enough particles land in the target’s class, or hold most of the prior mass, as the miscalibrated prior of Fig. 3 often does. The remaining errors are due to the models’ capability. In .13.13 to .49.49 of the runs no sampled program is consistent with the observed examples, and the CodeARC agent built on the same models reaches .06.06 to .30.30 (Tab. 1). Stronger models narrow this gap, with Qwen2.5-32B reaching the highest accuracy in every setting.

Appendix D Experimental Details

Infrastructure.

All models are served using vLLM33 3 https://docs.vllm.ai/en/, with tensor parallelism and GPU memory scaled to model size. Models up to 8B parameters were run on a single GPU, while 32B models used either four 24 GB GPUs in parallel or a single 96 GB GPU. All servers run vLLM’s batch-invariant kernels, so that seeded sampling is reproducible under concurrent load. Models are loaded in bfloat16. The algorithm’s sampling and query-selection loop runs on a separate CPU-only node and communicates with the model server over an SSH tunnel.

Model parameters.

We use M=64{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M}=64 particles, an evaluation set of size N=64{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}N}=64, resample when the effective sample size falls below τESS=4{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\tau_{\mathrm{ESS}}}=4, and terminate once a class holds more than half of the posterior mass. Runs that return a program observe 2.32.3 to 2.72.7 input–output examples on average, depending on the model. The query budget we use and report is 3030 input–output pairs, which includes the seed invocations. The evaluation set is shared across models. For each problem, we draw the evaluation set once from the input distribution μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu}, instantiated with Llama3.1-8B at temperature 1.11.1, conditioned on all 1010 seed invocations of the benchmark. The evaluation set therefore draws on seed examples that the algorithm does not see at 11 seed invocation. Its inputs coincide with a seed input in 0.3%0.3\% of the entries, and rebuilding it from the 55 visible seed examples changed the accuracy of Llama3.2-3B, Llama3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-32B by at most .02.02 on 100100 problems. Rebuilding it from the single visible seed example on the full split changes accuracy by at most .02.02 on five of six models and lowers that of Qwen2.5-32B from .342.342 to .280.280 (Tab. 3). Our method remains more accurate than the CodeARC agent on all models but Ministral-8B (p<.01p<.01, paired sign test) and observes fewer input–output examples on average on all but Qwen2.5-32B, as with the shared evaluation set. We keep the shared evaluation set for all settings. The guarantee of Prop. 2.1 is with respect to this input distribution. The proposal prompt and sampling temperature are selected per model on a screening set (§ E.6, Fig. 5), and the prompts are given in App. F. The maximum context length is capped at 12288 tokens across all models.

The CodeARC benchmark (Wei et al., 2025) is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-3B are released under the Llama 3.1 and Llama 3.2 Community Licenses respectively. Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B are released under the Apache 2.0 license. Olmo3-7B is released under the Apache 2.0 license, and Ministral-8B under the Mistral Research License.

Appendix E Additional Results

E.1 Failure Modes

Table 4 decomposes the runs of Tab. 1 by their terminal state to explain the gap between the correctness guarantee of Thm. 3.1 and the accuracies of Tab. 1. Most runs fail before the stopping rule applies. In a large share of them, between .13.13 and .49.49 depending on the model, no sampled program is consistent with the oracle’s answers, so the posterior is empty. In most of the remaining runs the posterior converges on a wrong program, owing to the proposal placing its mass on a plausible alternative that survives the few queries, as expected from the miscalibrated prior of Fig. 3. Runs that keep querying until the budget is exhausted are rare, so the query budget does not limit accuracy. Both failure modes stem from the proposal. Accordingly, the particle budget (§ E.5) and the prompt (§ E.6) affect accuracy more than the query selection strategy (Tab. 6).

E.2 Per-Instance Bound Analysis

Table 5 compares, run by run, the termination round of EIG with the bound of Thm. 3.2 evaluated on that run. The bound is attained in .37.37 of the runs, and is loose when the guaranteed information is not uniform over the queries of a run, since γ{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\gamma} is the minimum over the run’s queries and a single uninformative query loosens the bound.

E.3 Query Selection Strategies

Tab. 6 reports, per model, the quantities of Fig. 1 at the end of the run for every query selection strategy of Alg. 1 and for the CodeARC agent, together with the average information the selected queries are guaranteed to yield. All strategies score the same candidate inputs under the same weighted particle posterior and differ only in the score. EIG maximizes the estimated information gain about the equivalence class, Eq. 7. Uncertainty sampling maximizes the number of distinct outputs predicted by the particles of nonzero weight. Diversity maximizes the smallest character-trigram distance, one minus the Jaccard similarity, to the inputs already queried. Random draws an input uniformly. The strategies differ in the guaranteed information. EIG guarantees close to one bit per query, uncertainty sampling somewhat less, and diversity and random selection about half as much. This ordering carries over to the number of input–output examples, where the informed strategies save about one example per run against random selection, but not to accuracy, where all four strategies differ by at most .06.06 for every model. The accuracy of a run is decided by whether the proposal contains a correct program (§ E.1), which every strategy then finds within a few queries. The information criterion therefore saves oracle calls at the same accuracy. Against the CodeARC agent, it improves both for all models but Ministral-8B.

E.4 Controls and Literature Baselines

Tables 7, 8 and 9 separate the contributions of the importance weights, the selection rule, and the sampling budget. All runs use 11 seed invocation and 33 seeds, and stars mark a paired sign test over problems and seeds (p∗⁣∗<.01{}^{**}p<.01, ∗∗∗p<.001{}^{***}p<.001). Table 7 replaces the importance weights by uniform weights over consistent programs, as in Kobalczyk et al. (2025), and by the exact weights of the sampled completions. The latter requires sampling at temperature 11, so all three arms use it here. The approximate weights of § 4.2 and the exact weights perform on par, and both require significantly fewer input–output examples than uniform weights for all six models, at no significant difference in accuracy. Table 8 ports the selection rules of Ji et al. (2020) and Lee et al. (2025) (minimax with uniform weights) and of Kobalczyk et al. (2025) (EIG with uniform weights) into Alg. 1, keeping the proposal, evaluation set, and stopping rule fixed. Both require significantly more input–output examples than our method, at no significant difference in accuracy. Table 9 matches the sampling budget. A propose-and-verify baseline draws 112112 programs, the average number our method samples, keeps those consistent with the seed example, and returns a program of the majority class. Our method is significantly more accurate for five of six models.

E.5 Particle Budget

Fig. 4 varies the number of particles M{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M} from 22 to 256256 for three models on 100100 problems with 11 seed invocation. More particles produce more behavioral classes at round 11, so the first query is more informative, and the algorithm ends with fewer input–output examples and higher accuracy. Accuracy keeps rising past the M=64{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M}=64 of the main experiments and does not saturate at 256256, which agrees with the failure modes of § E.1, since the runs that converge on a wrong program or on none are runs in which no correct program was sampled, and a larger particle set samples one more often. We use 6464 to limit the per-round cost, which grows with the number of programs that have to be executed on S{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}S} (Tab. 2).

E.6 Proposal Prompt and Sampling Temperature

The proposal qt{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t} depends on the prompt shown to the LM and on its sampling temperature. We consider four prompts (Prompts A–D, App. F), which differ in how strongly they ask for hypotheses that disagree on unseen inputs, and six temperatures between 0.70.7 and 1.31.3. We choose the prompt and temperature for each model in a preliminary screen over prompts and temperatures in this range. The 100100 screening problems are part of the evaluation split. Recomputing Tab. 1 on the remaining 985985 problems changes every entry by at most .007.007. Figure 5 reports the accuracy of the full algorithm over the grid of prompts and temperatures. No prompt is best for every model. With about 100100 problems per configuration, differences of a few hundredths are within sampling noise. Ministral-8B degrades at temperatures above 1.11.1 and Llama3.2-3B performs worst with the shortest prompt (Prompt A), with accuracy varying by .18.18 and .15.15 across the grid for these two models, compared with .07.07 to .12.12 for the others.
